title: Removing grudges
hookLine: five ways to let go of a grudge: kindness, compassion, equanimity, not attending, remembering kamma

cards: A grudge can be big, or tiny: the coworker who took credit, the cousin who never paid back the forty dollars, the friend who didn't show up.
Someone can be in the shower, thinking about nothing, and suddenly they're arguing with that person again. Winning, usually. It's like a song stuck in your head that you didn't even like.
The Book of Fives has a short, very practical sutta for exactly this: a toolkit of five, for when resentment rises toward anyone.

teach.b: The Pali word here is aghata: resentment, ill will that keeps returning. When it arises toward someone, the sutta says, here are five ways to remove it.

First, develop loving-kindness toward that person: wish them well, on purpose, even a little. Second, if that's too much, compassion: see that they, too, are caught in suffering, maybe of their own making.
Third, equanimity: steady, even-minded, not swinging toward them or away. Fourth, simply stop paying attention to them.
Don't feed the thought; let them go out of focus, the way you stop hearing the refrigerator hum.

teach.h: THEY ARE HEIRS TO THEIR DEEDS.
teach.b: Fifth, apply kamma: this person is the owner of their deeds, heir to their deeds. Whatever they do, they will inherit. It's not your job to carry the bill.
Notice what the list is not. It doesn't say the other person was right. It doesn't say pretend nothing happened, or even make up with them.
It's about removing the thing from your own mind, where it's doing the real damage. And there are five, not one. If kindness won't come, try compassion; if neither will, try not attending.
Five tools leave room for the days when one won't work. Yesterday's line returns here, turned around: they are heirs to theirs.

how: Buddhist teachers often give the five ways of removing resentment as practical advice for lay people and monastics alike, and many traditions pair it with loving-kindness meditation directed toward a difficult person.

o: getting even, then calling it square
letting go of resentment, five ways

p: they are heirs to their own deeds

s: to remove a grudge, the sutta says you must make up with the person
it never says that; the five ways work on your own mind.
one of the five ways is simply to stop paying attention
not attending: let the person go out of focus.
the sutta offers only one method: loving-kindness
it offers five, so that when one won't work, another might.

games.q: you try to wish someone well, and you just can't today. what does the sutta suggest?
o: try another of the five, like compassion or not attending.
games.why: the sutta gives five tools on purpose. if kindness won't come, there's compassion, equanimity, not attending, or remembering kamma.

practice: Bring the person to mind lightly, at a distance, as if across a street, and notice what rises in the body: heat, tightness, a story starting.

Then pick one tool: wish them well in a few words, see the suffering they carry, rest evenly, or, if it's too raw today, let them fade from focus and come back to the breath. Whichever you choose is the right one for now.

wordCard.voice: Removing grudges. Five tools from the Book of Fives: loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, not paying attention, and remembering that each person is heir to their own deeds. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali aghata: resentment or malice, literally a striking or blow.

carryVoice: Your line: grudge removed. They keep their deeds, and you get your mind back. That's day six hundred sixty-six.
